summary: PSI has no combustion tests in partial gravity. Every PSI combustion test ran in microgravity, on the ISS or in a Cygnus cargo vehicle, and normal gravity on Earth is the other bound, so flame behaviour on the Moon (about 0.17 g) or Mars (about 0.38 g) lies between the two. The closest PSI data are ACME E-FIELD, where an electric field drives a flow that can stand in for buoyancy, and Saffire-II, which reports normal-gravity burn results beside its microgravity results for the same samples. The challenge brief names two planned experiments, LUCI and FM2, that are expected to add partial-gravity data.

stand_in.summary: ACME E-FIELD applied electric fields to flames in microgravity. The ions in the flame drive a flow that can stand in for buoyancy, so its results are the closest PSI data to partial gravity.

evidence.text: This unique environment is ideal for isolating electric field effects from buoyancy forces.
The electric field interacts with ions generated through chemi-ionization during combustion, driving ion-driving convection and influencing flame behavior.
Karnani, S. et al., Simulating Gravity in Microgravity Combustion Using Electric Fields, CST, 2012

BASS–II tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, O2 concentration, temperature, etc.).

The two main objectives for BASS are to: 1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity.
Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects.

The work further aimed to reconcile microgravity and normal gravity flame behavior, identify key physical and chemical processes influencing smoke point development, and provide a framework for evaluating model parameter sensitivity.

Microgravity conditions would produce longer, more diffuse flames with lower temperatures and increased soot concentrations compared to normal gravity, and that careful integration of experimental temperature fields into the simulations would reduce discrepancies between measured and predicted soot distributions.

Comparative analyses were also carried out with a parallel NSF-supported terrestrial flame spread project, ensuring that the predictive capabilities of the UFGM approach were assessed across both microgravity and normal-gravity conditions.

The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions.

Specifically, the hypothesis posits that the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions.

The objectives of this investigation were to: (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.

This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty.

Similar to the original SAME investigation, the primary objective of the SAME-R investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment.

In particular, it is hypothesized that liquid aerosol smokes produced in microgravity will exhibit substantially larger droplet sizes than under the same conditions in normal gravity (with a corresponding decrease in the particle number density for the same mass of smoke).
